items.readable_text:
Content:
We can use repeated matrix multiplication to determine the state of a system given its initial state and some information about how one state transitions to the next state.

Content:
To explain this concretely, suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

Content:
- [MATH: 6\%] of the city population relocates to the countryside,
- [MATH: 3\%] of the countryside population relocates to the city, and
- everyone else remains where they are.

Content:
This information can be represented using a diagram, like the one below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/607fa544e0da73963380a042ae01d18e]

Content:
We can also present this information as a table:

Content:
| | | From: |
| | | City | Countryside |
| To: | City | [MATH: 0.94] | [MATH: 0.03] |
| Countryside | [MATH: 0.06] | [MATH: 0.97] |

Content:
We want to use this information to determine how the population will be distributed [MATH: n] years after the study was carried out.

Content:
First, let's turn this table into a matrix [MATH: P\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [0.94|0.03; 0.06|0.97]]

Content:
Notice that this matrix has the following properties:

Content:
- it is a square matrix
- the sum of the entries in each column equals [MATH: 1]
- all entries in the matrix are non-negative

Content:
A square matrix with these properties is called a stochastic matrix.

Content:
Now suppose that, at the time of the study, [MATH: 70\%] of the population lived in the city and [MATH: 30\%] in the countryside. We can represent this initial state using a so-called stochastic vector [MATH: \mathbf x_0,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [0.70; 0.30]]

Content:
Stochastic vectors contain non-negative entries only, and the sum of the entries equals [MATH: 1.] Note that each column of [MATH: P] is a stochastic vector.

Content:
Now that we have our stochastic matrix and initial state vector, we can use matrix multiplication to calculate the population distribution sometime after the initial study took place:

Content:
- To calculate the population distribution after one year, we calculate the product [MATH: P\mathbf x_0\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [0.94|0.03; 0.06|0.97]]
The resulting vector
[MATH: [0.667; 0.333]]
tells us that one year after the study, [MATH: 66.7]% of the population will live in the city, and [MATH: 33.3]% will live in the countryside.
- To model the distribution after [MATH: 2] years, we compute [MATH: P\mathbf x_1\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [0.94|0.03; 0.06|0.97]]
The resulting vector
[MATH: [0.637; 0.363]]
tells us that two years after the study, [MATH: 63.7]% of the population will live in the city, and [MATH: 36.3]% will live in the countryside.

items.title: Identifying Stochastic Vectors and Stochastic Matrices

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

[MATH: [− 0.2|0; 1.2|1]]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

[MATH: [− 0.2|0; 1.2|1]]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to [MATH: 1.] A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

  • Matrix [MATH: \bf{U}] is not a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (it contains negative entries): [MATH: [− 0.2|0; 1.2|1]]

  • Matrix [MATH: \bf{V}] is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one): [MATH: [0.35|0.95; 0.65|0.05]0.35 + 0.65 = 1; 0.95 + 0.05 = 1]

  • Matrix [MATH: \bf{W}] is not a stochastic matrix since its third column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one): [MATH: [0|1|0; 0.5|0|0.4; 0.5|0|0.7]]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: \bf{V}] only."

To find the state vector corresponding to the [MATH: (k+1)]th year, we left-multiply the state vector corresponding to the [MATH: k]th year by [MATH: P.] This gives rise to the following sequence:

Content:
[MATH: x_{1}|= Px_{0},; x_{2}|= Px_{1},; x_{3}|= Px_{2},; ⋮|⋮; x_{k + 1}|= Px_{k}; ⋮|⋮]

Content:
A sequence of stochastic vectors [MATH: \mathbf{x}_0, \mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2, \ldots] related to a stochastic matrix [MATH: P] in this way is called a Markov chain.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We can use repeated matrix multiplication to determine the state of a system given its initial state and some information about how one state transitions to the next state.

Content:
To explain this concretely, suppose we have a population where people live either in the city or the countryside. A study carried out by the local authority shows that, each year,

Content:
- [MATH: 6\%] of the city population relocates to the countryside,
- [MATH: 3\%] of the countryside population relocates to the city, and
- everyone else remains where they are.

Content:
This information can be represented using a diagram, like the one below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/607fa544e0da73963380a042ae01d18e]

Content:
We can also present this information as a table:

Content:
| | | From: |
| | | City | Countryside |
| To: | City | [MATH: 0.94] | [MATH: 0.03] |
| Countryside | [MATH: 0.06] | [MATH: 0.97] |

Content:
We want to use this information to determine how the population will be distributed [MATH: n] years after the study was carried out.

Content:
First, let's turn this table into a matrix [MATH: P\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [0.94|0.03; 0.06|0.97]]

Content:
Notice that this matrix has the following properties:

Content:
- it is a square matrix
- the sum of the entries in each column equals [MATH: 1]
- all entries in the matrix are non-negative

Content:
A square matrix with these properties is called a stochastic matrix.

Content:
Now suppose that, at the time of the study, [MATH: 70\%] of the population lived in the city and [MATH: 30\%] in the countryside. We can represent this initial state using a so-called stochastic vector [MATH: \mathbf x_0,] given by

Content:
[MATH: [0.70; 0.30]]

Content:
Stochastic vectors contain non-negative entries only, and the sum of the entries equals [MATH: 1.] Note that each column of [MATH: P] is a stochastic vector.

Content:
Now that we have our stochastic matrix and initial state vector, we can use matrix multiplication to calculate the population distribution sometime after the initial study took place:

Content:
- To calculate the population distribution after one year, we calculate the product [MATH: P\mathbf x_0\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [0.94|0.03; 0.06|0.97]]
The resulting vector
[MATH: [0.667; 0.333]]
tells us that one year after the study, [MATH: 66.7]% of the population will live in the city, and [MATH: 33.3]% will live in the countryside.
- To model the distribution after [MATH: 2] years, we compute [MATH: P\mathbf x_1\mathbin{:}]
[MATH: [0.94|0.03; 0.06|0.97]]
The resulting vector
[MATH: [0.637; 0.363]]
tells us that two years after the study, [MATH: 63.7]% of the population will live in the city, and [MATH: 36.3]% will live in the countryside.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Stochastic Vectors and Stochastic Matrices

Example Prompt:
Which of the following are stochastic matrices?

[MATH: [− 0.2|0; 1.2|1]]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that a stochastic vector is a vector with nonnegative entries that add up to [MATH: 1.] A matrix is stochastic if all its columns are stochastic vectors.

With that in mind, let's examine our matrices in turn.

- Matrix [MATH: \bf{U}] is not a stochastic matrix since its first column is not a stochastic vector (it contains negative entries):
[MATH: [− 0.2|0; 1.2|1]]
- Matrix [MATH: \bf{V}] is a stochastic matrix. Indeed, each column is a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries are nonnegative and add up to one):
[MATH: [0.35|0.95; 0.65|0.05]0.35 + 0.65 = 1; 0.95 + 0.05 = 1]
- Matrix [MATH: \bf{W}] is not a stochastic matrix since its third column is not a stochastic vector (the corresponding entries don't add up to one):
[MATH: [0|1|0; 0.5|0|0.4; 0.5|0|0.7]]

Therefore, the correct answer is "[MATH: \bf{V}] only."

---

Item 5 — Example: Constructing a Stochastic Matrix Given Some Data

Example Prompt:
There are two groups of people in a particular city: those who use their own vehicles and those who use public transport. A study has shown that, each year

- [MATH: 35\%] of people who used their own vehicles swap to public transport, and
- [MATH: 25\%] of people who used public transport swap to their own vehicles.

Give the stochastic matrix that describes how people change their means of transportation each year.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We are given the following situation for each year:

- [MATH: 35\%] of people who used their own vehicles swap to public transport. This implies that [MATH: 65\%] of them remain using their own vehicles.
- [MATH: 25\%] of people who used public transport swap to their own vehicles. This implies that [MATH: 75\%] of them remain using public transport.

Writing this information in tabular form, we obtain the following:

| | | From: |
| | | Vehicles | Public Transport |
| To: | Vehicles | [MATH: 0.65] | [MATH: 0.25] |
| Public Transport | [MATH: 0.35] | [MATH: 0.75] |

Note that we can write a corresponding stochastic matrix as follows:
[MATH: [0.65|0.25; 0.35|0.75]]

Item 12 — Example: Constructing a Stochastic Matrix and Making a Prediction

Example Prompt:
A certain industry produces [MATH: 2] types of sugar, namely sugar [MATH: A] and sugar [MATH: B]. The following table describes how the number of consumers changes between both types of sugar in a month:

| | | From: |
| | | Sugar [MATH: A] | Sugar [MATH: B] |
| To: | Sugar [MATH: A] | [MATH: 0.3] | [MATH: 0.45] |
| Sugar [MATH: B] | [MATH: 0.7] | [MATH: 0.55] |

That is, [MATH: 70\%] of sugar [MATH: A] customers switch to sugar [MATH: B] each month, and [MATH: 45\%] of sugar [MATH: B] customers switch to sugar [MATH: A.]

Currently, [MATH: 600] customers use sugar [MATH: A,] while [MATH: 400] customers use sugar [MATH: B.] How many customers will use sugar [MATH: A] in one month? You may assume that the total number of customers doesn't change.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
From the table, we can build the corresponding stochastic matrix:

[MATH: [0.3|0.45; 0.7|0.55]]

The vector describing the number of customers for each type of sugar is
[MATH: [600; 400]]
Dividing the vector above by the total number of customers [MATH: (1\,000),] we get the stochastic vector of the initial state:

[MATH: [600; 400]]

To find the state vector [MATH: \mathbf{x}_1] after one month, we apply one step of the Markov chain:

[MATH: \mathbf{x}_1=P\mathbf{x}_0]

Therefore, we have

[MATH: x_{1}|= Px_{0}; = [0.3|0.45; 0.7|0.55][0.6; 0.4]; = [0.36; 0.64].]

So, after one month, [MATH: \color{blue}36\%] of customers will use sugar [MATH: A.] Computing [MATH: 36\%] of [MATH: 1\,000,] we obtain

[MATH: 1\,000 \cdot 0.36 = 360.]

Therefore, [MATH: 360] customers will use sugar [MATH: A] in one month.
